response.sql:
WITH gender_counts AS (
  SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count
  FROM Invoices i
  JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
  JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.gender
),
shares AS (
  SELECT gender, order_count, CAST(order_count AS REAL) / SUM(order_count) OVER () AS share
  FROM gender_counts
),
avg_share AS (
  SELECT AVG(share) AS avg_share FROM shares
)
SELECT s.gender, s.order_count, s.share, s.share - a.avg_share AS share_minus_avg
FROM shares s
CROSS JOIN avg_share a
WHERE s.share > a.avg_share;

assumptions.assumption: Invoices are linked to Orders and Customers with inner joins, so invoices whose order or customer has no matching row are dropped; each order is counted once via COUNT(DISTINCT order_id).
Customers with a NULL gender form their own group, which counts toward the total and the average share. The request does not say whether NULL is a 'gender'.
Gender values are used as stored, with no case or whitespace normalization (for example 'F' and 'f' are separate groups).

alternatives.interpretation: Exclude customers with a NULL gender, so only non-null gender values form the groups, the total, and the average share.

WITH gender_counts AS (
  SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count
  FROM Invoices i
  JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
  JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  WHERE c.gender IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY c.gender
),
shares AS (
  SELECT gender, order_count, CAST(order_count AS REAL) / SUM(order_count) OVER () AS share
  FROM gender_counts
),
avg_share AS (
  SELECT AVG(share) AS avg_share FROM shares
)
SELECT s.gender, s.order_count, s.share, s.share - a.avg_share AS share_minus_avg
FROM shares s
CROSS JOIN avg_share a
WHERE s.share > a.avg_share;
